When one gazes upon the venerable form of my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Crothers). it is somewhat difficult to believe he is still a boy, but as one listens, the difficulty disappears. A gentleman who can imagine that he can carry on a tariff discussion by abandoning what he calls treacherous figures and'bv addressing himself instead to mountains, valleys, forests and streams, is giving the best proof that he is not yet past his boyhood. A gentleman who imagines that he can substitute strutting phrases for sound arguments and that, by making ibroad declarations, he can establish sane conclusions is, I think, entitled to all the benefit he can obtain from the most extreme youth.
My hon. friend wondered why the hon. member for Bed Deer (Mr. Clark) addressed some of his arguments to the opposition. Well, it is perfectly plain that arguments of that kind, like sermons, are usually addressed to the vilest sinners in the hope of accomplishing most good, and one cannot doubt that the arguments in question are more needed on the opposition than on the government side of the House. My hon. friend from Bed Deer pointed out that the whole policy of the Liberal government has been in the direction of an endeavour to secure a broader measure of free trade to this country. Whereas the policy on the other side has been exactly the reverse. But now we have my hon. friend (Mr. Crothers), who has just taken his seat, saying that the policy which has been the cause of such immense success in our manufacturing industries is that which was initiated by the late Conservative administration. Well, let me invite the attention of the hon. gentleman to the language used by Sir Charles Tupper, the leader of the Conservative party and by the hon. member for North Toronto, (Mr. Foster) with regard to the Fielding tariff. That language was to the effect that the Fielding tariff was of such a character that it would utterly ruin Mr. CROTHERS.
and destroy the industries of this country. It was easy enough for those hon. gentlemen then, to make that prophecy, to point out that nothing but misery and ruin would follow; and it is just as easy now, when the very reverse is shown to have followed, to say that the tariff inaugurated in 1896 by this government was nothing but the old Conservative tariff. The hon. gentleman then claimed the distinction for his party of having initiated the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway,. but it does seem to me that the Mackenzie government which was in power before" 1878, had something to do with the construction of a road that corresponds with the Canadian Pacific railway. And the Mackenzie administration then initiated a policy with regard to the construction of railways which was much more in the interests of the country than the one subsequently followed. No one can doubt that the building of the Canadian Pacific railway has worked great benefits to Canada. No one can doubt that it has done much to open up our Northwest, but it must not be forgotten that that road had been opened twelve years before the present government came to power and that, until the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) became Minister of the Interior and substituted for the old antique methods, modern, scientific, active and energetic efforts, there was absolutely no development commensurate with what the people had a right to expect from the great sacrifices they had made. And the end is not yet with regard to the injuries inflicted by the Canadian Pacific railway. If I am correctly informed that company, by virtue of the policy which hon. gentlemen opposite are responsible for, is now in possession of the alternate sections on the Grand Trunk Pacific and propose to hold the sections up and not sell them, merely in order to ruin the Grand Trunk Pacific. That is the policy which my hon. friend (Mr. Crothers) lauds so highly. It is one which has been a curse throughout the Northwest and is a curse to-day and will be more and more a curse as the country opens up.
It seems to me that my hon. friend differs somewhat from the hon. gentleman for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) with regard to the appearance of affairs at present. The hon. member for North Toronto, in his * desperate gloom and horrible despondency, could see nothing cheerful except the countenance of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). Well, I think that most people in this country would like to see some of the cheerfulness exhibited in the countenance of the Minister of Finance reflected in the countenance and language of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster).
The time has passed when it is wise for any man in this country to speak of the
1S05

affairs of Canada as being ' in a slough of despond.' I venture to say that there is no man who knows anything about our affairs-except the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster)-who would speak of the affairs of this country being now or having been at any time recently in anything like a slough of despond. There never was a time when Canada was more prosperous or more hopeful than at the present day. And the only man in this House, who does not realize that appears to be the hon. member for North Toronto. In order to make a point he said that, in the budget of 1908-9 the Finance Minister, instead of curtailing instead of trimming sail for the storm which every man saw approaching, he had continued under full sail risking disaster. It is not well for the captain who has been dismissed from his employment by reason of not being able to carry the ship of state through the Storms to criticise another captain who has been successful on the ground that in such and such emergencies something might have happneed through his carrying too much sail. The member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) said:
The minister might have added to the financial position of this country very materially if he had done as every business man in the country did, as the chancellor of every exchequer that I know of did, as any prudent business man would do-curtail in the face of the storm that was yet to come and so save in that way what he could of the strength and credit of the country's finances.
Now, Sir, I do not know as much about the chancelleries of the world as the hon. member for North Toronto. Yet, I begin to think that even he does not know as much about them as his language would indicate. For, if he had gone to the budgets of Great Britain and the United States he would have found that the very contrary to that which he stated was the fact -that the masters of those ships of state, had the same confidence in their crafts to weather the financial storm that was approaching-and with as much reason as shown by the result-as had our Minister of Finance in the Dominion of Canada. For, in that year, and in the subsequent year, both in Great Britain and in the United States, not only the estimated but the actual expenditure exceeded any previous year except one from 1905 to that time.
Now, the hon. member for North Toronto is even despondent about the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. I do not see how any one who looks at the condition of affairs in the new provinces and in the Northwest Territories can doubt the wisdom of the policy which is endeavouring-and is succeeding -to provide for this country another great transcontinental railway. Not only was such construction necessary in view of
the enlargement of the country and in view of the necessity of saving the great Northwest Territories of Canada from falling absolutely into the hands of the Canadian Pacific railway, but it was necessary in order to provide for the enormous development which was foreseen. And I venture to say that we are on the eve, as soon as that road is opened, of the most marvellous material and commercial development known in the history of the Dominion. You see, here and there, small towns which undoubtedly will blossom forth into large cities; you see villages ready to become towns; and from the Atlantic to the Pacific the whole Dominion will undoubtedly receive a great impetus from the construction of that road. It would not be surprising if the policy of the government should finally lead to the extension of that road to the port of Halifax. The eastern provinces, I believe, are in as hopeful a condition as ever they were and will soon begin to reap, more than they have done heretofore, some measure of the benefit of this prosperity spreading over the Dominion. There is nothing to hinder the Atlantic Canadian port, either Halifax or St. John-Halifax, I believe, for it seems to me to have been designed by nature as the seaport of the largest portion of the trade of the Dominion-I say I do not think there is anything that will hinder Halifax and St. John on the Atlantic and Vaueouver, Victoria or Prince Rupert or all of them, from being centres of as large a freight and passenger traffic as ever has been in the history of the world. How any hon. member can entertain any doubt with regard to the benefit that will accrue to this country from the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway entirely passes my comprehension. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) has dealt with another feature of the speech of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster)-the question of the balance of trade. If the argument advanced not only by the hon. member for North Toronto, but also by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie) and some others in this House is correct, if it be really an adverse balance of trade for us to have more imports than exports, and if the favourable condition of trade be an excess of exports over imports, then India to-day is a prosperous country and Great Britain is very much the reverse. For, as pointed out by the hon. member for Red Deer, the imports of Great Britain for years and decades have exceeded the exports, whereas the exports of India for as many years have exceeded the imports. I believe that the reason can be found in the words of Fawcett-and I would invite the attention of my hon. friend from North Simcoe to some of portions of the works on political economy that he has been reading and ask

him to give some attention to what they say on the subject of the balance of trade upon which he talked a great deal tout concerning which, apparently, he had not taken the trouble to read the very authorities to which he referred. Fawcett.said:
if a country is in debt to other countries her exports will exceed in value her imports by an amount equivalent to her annual indebtedness. If, on the other hand, a country should be a creditor and not a debtor of other countries, the value of her imports will exceed that of her exports by an amount which will be equivalent' to the indebtedness of other countries to her.
Now, it is perfectly apparent that Great Britain is a great creditor nation. Other countries all over the world must pay interest on their indebtedness to Great Britain, and the only way in which they can pay it is in the form of exports from their own countries which become imports into Great Britain, making an excess of imports into Great Britain. Most of the other political economists with whom I am acquainted- and I have been realing up the subject- claim that this idea of an adverse balance of trade is a foolish and exploded notion. As Blanqui says, it is ' proved a vagary.' Why, if there were anything in it the Minister of Customs and the Minister of the Interior make a very serious mistake in not instructing their officials all along the international boundary to meet the Americans coming into this country and say: ' Gentlemen, you can come in but you must not bring in your effects, for if you bring them in you will swell the adverse balance of trade against Canada.' One can understand that if you take some particular item of trade you might possibly say that, in regard to that particular item, it is desirable that our exports should exceed our imports-though, I must say I cannot think of anything of which that would be true. But to talk of the whole trade of a country and say that, because the imports exceed the exports, that country has an adverse balance of trade, appears to me a vagary which, if not exploded, ought to be exploded very shortly. Let me point out one way in which this so-called adverse balance of trade is swollen. In the Yukon territory, several million dollars worth of mining machinery has been imported and set up, machinery of a kind not now manufactured in Canada. To wait fox the development of that country until the machinery was manufactured in Canada would mean the absolute abandonment of the country for many years. Consequently, I think every one will recognize the wisdom of going abroad to get the machinery, to hasten the development of the mining industry. The imports of Canada are swollen by the amount of the value of that machinery. Does any one say that it is not a desirable thing for Canada to purchase abroad Mr. CONGDON.
the mining machinery that is required in the Yukon territory in order to start min- [DOT] ing operations, and thus give employment to a large number of labouring men, increase the business of every merchant and every person engaged in business in that country, although it does create what the bon. gentlemen call an adverse balance of trade?
Another thing I wish to mention and that is trade between Canada and the United States. I have always frankly expressed my views on that question. Now, Sir, while I am as loyal a British subject as there is, I have the very highest regard and esteem also for the republic to the south of us, and I believe that the greatest function that Canada can perform, in her own interest and that of the empire, is to assist to bring about the most friendly relations between Great Britain and the United States of America. Speak of a fiscal policy which would make Canada an annex of the Uniteu States! What ridiculous nonsense! Do you imagine that because we are carrying on trade which is profitable both to Canada and the United States, therefore we must become annexed to the greater country? For my part I believe that the most desirable condition of Canada would be one of absolute freedom of commercial intercourse with the United States. Our social relations, our commercial relations and all other relations should be of the most friendly character. I say that so far from involving any danger of our political entity being absorbed in that of the United States, it would be postponing it, removing the danger of any such fusion of the two countries. There is a large and growing portion of the people of the United States who realize that our country- is a magnificent example of an endeavour to carry on republican institutions. They are a republican democracy, we are a monarchial democracy. We believe, and some of them believe, that under our system of government we are accomplishing greater freedom for the community and for individuals even than they are in the United States; and the wisest, the sanest, and the most advanced minds in the United States realize that it may be well on this continent for two independent nations to exist side by side, aiming at the same object, the attainment of the best interests of the whole people, that these two experiments should be conducted concurrently, one learning from the other, so that if one fails in tne experiment the other may take warning by the failure, and avoid the errors that led to it. So far from intimate and close trade relations between Canada and the United States involving any danger to our political institutions, I believe, and I think I am supported by all who have studied the

question carefully, that such relations will advance the interests of Canada and tend to our continued separation as a political entity.
Now hon. gentlemen think that it is a horrible thing that trade between Canada and the United states is greater than trade between Canada and Great Britain. Sir, the result is inevitable, and is a consequence of the ordinary movement of trade currents. Trade naturally follows meridians rather than parallels of latitude, for the simple reason that in pursuing parallels of latitude you are trading with a country similarly situated, whereas when trade follows meridians it is reaching out to countries differently situated, having different products, performing the mission which Tennyson ascribes to commerce ' to mix the seasons and the golden hours.' That doctrine is as applicable to Canada as it is to the rest of the world. It has been well established throughout the rest of the world; and, try as much as you please, give as great a preference as you will to Great Britain, it will not be possible for this country to make trade with any other country in the world which will exceed the trade of Canada with the United States. For my part I welcome it, believing as I do, that it is one of the best things that can happen, not only to Canada but to the United States, and that the soundest trade policy is one which will be as beneficial to the one country as to the other.
There was one portion of the address of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) to which I wish to direct the especial attention of the House, not that that it is a matter in which this House is especially interested, because I have found a most wonderful lack of interest in eastern Canada in anything relating to the northern part of Canada. The residents of eastern Canada, and also of western Canada, for that matter, are so deeply engaged in the development of their own sections of the country that they take very little interest in anything beyond. The common notion with regard to the Yukon territory, or of any other part of our northern territory, is that it is a great barren wilderness filled with icebergs, behind which the inhabitants are dodging and trying to keep themselves from freezing to death. A greater misconception never existed. The hon. member for North Toronto has never been able, in any speech made in this House, to mention the Yukon territory, or the officials, or the people, of the Yukon, without saying something derogatory of them. He knows no more about the Yukon territory, about the conditions there, than Balaam's ass knew about Hebrew grammar. Now, the hon. gentleman tries to belittle the Yukon territory by saying that it has a population of less than 8,000, probably 5,000. If it has only 5,000, I say they are one of the most remarkable 5,000 that have ever been collected together in any part of this mundane sphere. Imagine what would happen in the rest of Canada if every unit of 5,000 people added so greatly to the wealth of the country as the 5,000 people in the Yukon territory. Last year, and for several years before that, the gold production of the Yukon territory fell off. It was absolutely inevitable that it should fall off. In the earlier days there happened in the Yukon territory what happened in every other mining camp. Men flocked into the richest spots and these were capable of being easily worked. Men who knew nothing of mining, only enough to dig a hole in the ground, found a gold yield sufficient to make their fortune. But that ground naturally gets worked out in time, and if you could live in the Yukon territory and visit that ground which yielded these immense fortunes, you would still see gold bearing ground which I believe is richer than in any other part of the civilized world. The area which can be worked to-day is ten times as large as the area which could be worked nine or ten years ago. The area that can be profitably worked is increasing in extent and, is so enormous that its output only depends upon the cheapness with which it can be worked. Now hon. gentlemen should remember this fact. He blames this government for the falling off of the gold yield in the Yukon. I do not think the hon. gentleman seriously meant to say that, but perhaps he did. But I say that the falling off of the gold production was exactly what has happened in every other country between the first wild rush when riches are dug out easily, and the second stage when scientific methods are necessary to get the gold out of the ground. Last year our production in the Yukon was a little over two millions, this year it has jumped up to $3,662,000. I venture to say that for the next ten years you wall see an annual increase in the production of gold from placer ground alone with a continued improvement in the_ scientific mode of mining.
Now with regard to the government of the Yukon, and the reflections made by the hon. member on the government of that territory. It must be remembered that in the beginning of the Yukon territory there occurred one of the most remarkable movements of men that has occurred since the Children of Israel started out from Egypt on their famous wanderings in search of easier work than making bricks without straw. That movement differed from all other movements that I know of. We had a large body of men moving together. Other movements of

men were homogeneous; they were composed of men of the same language and the same ideas, and because of that fact it was easier to control and manage them than a movement such as this in which were represented every nation of the world, every trade, every profession, every occupation and every degree of morality. We had the pious deacon and the pickpocket and we had the preacher deserting for a time his sacred calling in the hope of being able to add to his poor stipend by striking a good claim, and men of every description. The worst feature of the ' crowd, numbering about one hundred thousand, was that while there were splendid men amongst it-no better could be found in the world-and while the large majority was eminently fit, capable, respectable and good, there was a lack of confidence in one section of the crowd with respect to the others. The individuals did not know one another. It might be that a man in a little group knew the members of that group but he knew nothing whatever about other groups, and the consequence was that the crowd that rushed in there was filled with distrust of itself and of its different constituents. This naturally created in the government of this country, being guided, I suppose, by the reports of the authorities who had the management of the Yukon, a distrust which was likely to grow. I do not think that any government will be greatly blamed it if takes pains to maintain the integrity of its territory. That is one thing that every government, whether British or Canadian, will protect. No government will take any chance in regard to the integrity of its territory. This government took no chance with regard to maintaining the Yukon territory as a territory of the Dominion of Canada. It sent into that country a force which I think was needless. But, it is easy to be wise after the event. Those 155 battleships that the British government 'scrapped' a few years ago were unnecessary but at the time they were constructed they were not deemed unnecessary. They served a purpose and the fact that they were ultimately 'scrapped' is no condemnation of the action of the government in constructing them at a time when they were believed to be necessary. This government sent into the territory a large force of the Northwest Mounted Police. No better force could have been sent, although I am not given to overpraise of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police or any other body of men. I realize that they have their faults and failings. In addition they sent in a large field force. That field force cost Canada $721,737. That was merely the result of the foresight of the Dominion Mr. CONGDON.
government in taking such measures as would ensure the retention of the Yukon territory to the Dominion of Canada. In the public accounts the cost is included as a charge against the Yukon territory. I do not think it is a fair item to include to make up the deficit to which the hon. member for North Toronto referred. At the time the Yukon territory was first opened up there was no idea that there would be any danger of an attempt to wrest that territory from the Dominion. It was at that time that the statement was made in this parliament that the Yukon would be made to pay for itself. There are some extraordinary expenditures which, as a matter of book-keeping, have been charged to the Yukon, but which are of such a character that they should not have been so charged. One is the $721,000 that is charged against the Yukon with respect to the field force. If there were danger of an invasion of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Ontario or any other part of the Dominion, and the Dominion government, in its wisdom and foresight, thought it necessary to incur an expense of that kind in order to ensure that portion of the Dominion against that danger, no one would think of charging that up t-o the particular province in which the danger arose. It would be treated as a national charge. And so, I say in regard to this charge, that the Canadian field force sent into the Yukon should not ibe considered as a charge against the Yukon. The Yukon did not ask for it, a good many people in there did not think it was necessary, and it was because [DOT]the authorities of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police and others thought there was some danger from the promiscuous character of the people and the surrounding country of an attempt to wrest the Yukon from Canada that this force was sent in. So in regard to the expenditure upon the Royal Northwest Mounted Police in the Yukon territory. It is easy enough to say now that there was no excuse for expending upon that force the large amount shown in the Public Accounts. We are charged with an expenditure of five million and some hundreds of thousands of dollars upon the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. You will find that the major part of the expense was incurred during the few years when this danger of an attack upon the Yukon was feared-I do not mean an international attack but an attack from filibusters, and during that time the force was kept at a strength that certainly was not necessary to maintain order within the country. In regard to the expense of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police in the Yukon territory, it is reasonable and fair to charge against that territory the proportion of the expense of such a force as would be necessary to

maintain order within the territory. But the expense of that portion which was kept there as a sort of precaution against the danger of an attempt upon the country is a portion which should be charged not against the Yukon but should be considered a national charge, and 1 do hope that the Minister of Finance will so rectify these accounts in this regard. It was most natural to put them where they were put in the first instance, but they should not now be considered as charges against the Yukon. When one comes to ask for some vote for the Yukon, member after member will get up and say that the Yukon has been a loss to Canada instead of a profit, thus illustrating the unfairness of charging these extraordinary expenditures to that territory. In addition to that we are charged, not only with the original capital cost of the telegraph, but with the whole annual cost. I find that $600,000 of the cost was for the portion of the line in the province of British Columbia. Last year the expenses of operating that line were, in the Yukon territory, $62,000, and the total cost of operating it in British Columbia was $158,000. Although our cost was only $62,000 wre are charged with $220,000. The total cost of constructing the telegraph line was something over $700,000; the cost of the portion in British Columbia was $600,000. That should he deducted. The cost of operating that line since its initiation in 1901 up to the present time has been $1,770,000, of which $500,000 have been expended in the Yukon, and have been charged against the Yukon. The way this occurs in regard to the telegraph is that originally it was treated as the Yukon system, and ever since all the expense incurred in British Columbia or anywhere else in connection with the Yukon telegraph system including even the branch line from Hazelton to Prince Rupert has been charged to the Yukon territory. I think the account should undergo revision in order to bring into it only those items which are legitimately and properly chargeable against the Yukon. I find in addition that $283,000, the amount paid as damages to Mackenzie and Mann are charged to the Yukon territory. I do not think it is fair to take that amount into consideration in estimating whether the Yukon has been a source of loss or profit to the Dominion of Canada. By including these various amounts the hon. member for North Toronto showed that the deficit of the Yukon amounted to $2,300,000. I think if that account were corrected in the way I have indicated and in the way that, I submit to the Finance Minister and this House, is the proper and legitimate way to correct it, it will be found that the Yukon has a surplus of over $3,500,000. In addition to that I wish to point out that it is utterly impossible to take the Yukon territory, or any other section of Canada, and make out from the public accounts the cost or benefit to the country of that particular section accurately and properly. The hon. member for North Toronto was surprised that while in 1900 and 1901 we had a surplus we had later used that up. _ The government of this country adopted' with the concurrence, with the express approval of the members of this House, a mistaken policy in the first place in respect to the Yukon Territory which was only corrected about 1901. It is the same policy as is being adopted to-day in the province of Ontario and, without any reflection on the motives for the enforcement of that policy, I repeat that it is a mistaken one. It is based on the idea that the rest of the country can take a large mining district and make money out of it for the other public services of the country. That is not right, it is not the correct policy with regard to any large mining territory to im-pose_ any taxes in addition to those which are imposed on the whole country and to expect that the rest of the country and not that particular territory will get the benefit o^ the special taxes so imposed. I think that a very few years will demonstrate the lack of wisdom, for instance of the province of Ontario, in thinking it can take such a large royalty from the mining production of Cobalt and other regions, and that the rest of Ontario outside those regions can derive any advantage from that royalty. Ontario will find a little later, when she has had more experience, that while it may be wise and proper to impose some measure of royalty upon the minerals produced in those districts it is absolutely essential that the income thus derived should be expended exclusively for the benefit of the districts from which it came. Down to 1901, the idea of this parliament and the idea generally prevailing was that these enormous sums of money that were coming out of the Yukon Territory should, some of them, find their way into the exchequer of Canada for the benefit of the rest of Canada, and as I say it was not until 1901 that this government realized, and adopted a policy founded on that realization, that the only sane and proper use to make of the royalty got from the Yukon territory was to devote it to local uses in the Yukon. Previous to that time we had no public building, the telegraph line was not constructed, we had no roads which are the absolutely essential needs of that country, and whatever large expenditure there was after 1900 was due to the fact that the government, as I think, realized that the royalty which they had received from that territory ought to be devoted to the development of that country. They adopted that policy and expended for these objects the surpluses which they had

previously piled up and the surplus of that year.	.
There are several causes which account i!or the reduction in the revenue from the Yukon since that time. In the first place, the royalty in the Yukon territory was ten percent, which was subsequently reduced to five per cent and later to two and a half. Necessarily the year in which the royalty was reduced from ten per cent to five per cent showed a decrease in the revenue, and this decrease was still greater when the royalty was reduced to two and a half per cent. Then, in the beginning of the Yukon, the people of Canada made a greater mistake than any mistake which the government made. They were not very familiar with mining localities, and made the great mistake of imagining that anything was good enough for a mining camp, whereas any one who knows anything about mining camps knows that nothing is too good for them. The miners have the money and will pay for good articles, especially if they are far away from commercial centres, because the cost of transportation is so great that they have adopted the wise policy of buying the very best. For instance, some Canadian manufacturers or merchants sent into the Yukon butter not fit for axle grease, and it took four or five years to get over the bad impression. created in the Yukon by that horrible butter; only in recent years would people in that country eat Canadian butter which they now find as good as any produced in the world. That is one matter in which the farmers, or who.ever were responsible for the butter made a mistake. Another matter in which the Canadian manufacturers erred was in respect to boilers. The country needed thousands of boilers. I have seen the streets of Dawson for half a mile piled up with small boilers and hoisting machinery. I came to manufacturers in the east and I know others came and asked them to meet that requirement of the Yukon and manufacture suitable boilers. Their answer was that their business was booming so rapidly that they could not undertake that business. One said that his business in the previous year had been so increased that he was obliged to double his capacity and if he attempted to fill the demand of the Yukon he would be obliged to still further increase his power of production and as a consequence he did not attempt to supply that market, and I venture to say that not one-half of one-quarter per cent of the boilers and hoisting machinery that went into that country came from Canada; it all came from the 'United States. The people of the Yukon -were quite willing to buy in this country and made endeavours to buy here, but when Canada would not furnish the articles demanded, they were obliged to turn elsewhere.

Another cause of reduction in the revenue from the Yukon is the change of the customs, and if I may express my opinion on
the subject I hope that the Ministers of Finance and Customs will recommend a further change, because I think there is no policy which can be wiser for Canada to pursue than the policy of making absolutely free those articles of machinery, those articles of necessity which go into a new country and are absolutely essential to build up its industries. Take the conditions in the Yukon. A mining proposition is of necessity always hazardous, and I maintain that as little taxation as possible should be imposed until the venture has been absolutely set afoot and has been proved to be a profitable one. By imposing large taxation at the beginning, you are crippling and perhaps rendering impossible an industry. Take for instance an industry that proposes to instal a large power plant to work mining machinery. It requires, in the first place, a large sum of money for installation. It is told that there is a heavy tariff on all machinery which it is required to import. That, of course, gives a little black eye to the scheme of promotion and then the promoters are obliged to pay a duty on that machinery at a time -when their industry has not produced anything and is not in a position to produce anything, and when the promoters are not absolutely certain it will not be a failure. In one respect a royalty is the best of all taxes on a mining territory, because a man is only asked to pay when he has the money in his pocket to pay. A tariff on mining machinery is the worst form of taxation, because it is a tax at the very initiation of an industry, which may and does stop thousands of developments that otherwise would take place.
Another cause of reduction in revenue in the Yukon, is due to the increased proportion of Canadian manufactured products used in that country. In the earlier days the major part of the importations into the Yukon was of American origin. I shall not weary the House with figures, but, for instance, in 1899 the domestic importations into the Yukon amounted to only 9,800 odd tons. By St. Michael's there were imported 3,334 tons and via Whitehorse, 6,510 tons, a total of 9,844. Of foreign importations via St. Michael's, there were 12.000 tons, and via Whitehorse, 2,700 tons, making a total of foreign importations of 15,000 tons against 9,800 tons of domestic importations, the total importatons at that time being 24,856. Every effort was made by the Department of Customs and by every one in that country who had any authority to direct the trade of the Yukon territory into Canadian channels, and this effort was successful to the extent that in 1906 the do-

mestic importations into the Yukon were 14,309, and the foreign 10,698, so that you have about the same gross importations, but the proportions of Canadian and foreign goods are reversed between 1899 and 1906. The change in the source of the goods imported into the Yukon necessarily caused a falling off in the customs revenue from that territory, even although some of those goods that appear as domestic may be foreign. But let me _give one instance to show how difficult it is to get at the exact revenue which the national treasury receives from any particular portion of Canadian territory. There is being installed about 40 or 50 miles below _ Dawson a large power plant which will distribute that power to Dawson and its vicinity, and furnish power which is absolutely essential for mining purposes. The company promoting that power plant were unable to make arrangements for the transportation of its machinery with the railway company that runs into the Yukon territory, and which I may say is the most horrible incubus that any country has ever laboured under. The power company were compelled to land their machinery at Vancouver, _ so that the province of British Columbia gets the credit for the revenue of $58,000 from the duty on that machinery, which is intended for and will eventually go to the Yukon. Of course it makes no difference so far as the revenue of the country as a whole is concerned, but if the Minister of Customs can find any way to credit that amount to the Yukon territory rather than to the province of British Columbia, I suggest that he should adopt it. That, however, is only one instance, and there are very many others of a similar kind which go to prove the suggestion with which I began, that it is impossible to show the revenue derived from any one section of the dominion. For example, I am informed that the customs revenue paid in the city of Montreal is one-third of the whole customs revenue of the Dominion of Canada, and while Montreal is a great city in a great province, yet there is no doubt that a very large part of the revenue paid there should be credited to other provinces in which the consumers who use the goods are located. In the same way, British Columbia gets credit for some of the revenue which should rightly be credited to the Yukon territory.
There is one other thing which I wish to say with regard to the Yukon territory before concluding my remarks, and that is that I think the government has adopted a correct policy in reducing to the very lowest possible amount the expenditure on the official administration of that territory. At one time undoubtedly the whole official staff employed in the Yukon was needed, and it is not an easy thing to
determine the exact moment when a change in conditions renders it no longer necessary to retain the whole staff previously existing. However, I think that now the time has arrived when the official staff in the Yukon territory should be reduced, and I say that out of no spite or malice against any of the officials. I believe it has been intimated that I secured the dismissal of some of them for political reasons. Indeed, it has been stated in a despatch to the public press that they had incurred my displeasure because they refused to give $50 each as a contribution to a political campaign fund. Although, some newspapers have published that despatch, I notice that when these gentlemen who are alleged to have made the change were interviewed in Vancouver, if they were ever interviewed, they made no such statement as that credited to them. At all events I invite any hon. member of this House who wishes to investigate the charge, to go to any or all of these officials and I think he will find they will deny that they ever made such a statement. I might add that I never made a request from them or from any man in my life for a contribution to my own or to any other campaign fund, and any one who knows me knows that I am one of the worst collectors that ever appeared in any country; I cannot collect even my own debts not to speak of collecting campaign funds. I may point out also that not one of the gentlemen who have been dismissed in the Yukon territory has had his place supplied by another oflficial. He was dismissed simply for the purpose of economizing, and so far from having any malice against them 1 have been eager to induce the government to adopt a system by which when it becomes necessary to get rid of an official in the Yukon he shall not be set adrift like an old horse but that he shall be transferred to some other branch of the service of the government, corresponding perhaps to the service he was in in the Yukon territory. I hbpe the members of the government will endeavour to carry out that idea, so that these officials may be transferred from places where they are not needed to offices where their services will be of benefit to the country. I am particularly desirous of reducing the expenses of administration in the Yukon in order that there may be a larger amount available for developing the resources of that rich country. I could spend hours, Mr. Speaker, dilating on the possibilities of the Canadian Yukon. _ There are I know some who imagine that its days of prosperity have passed, but I can assure them that the beginning of the development of the Yukon has not yet come. I am supported in this belief by those who know the territory best and who declare that the

output from placer gold mining will increase year by year for many years to come. It will continue beyond the life of even the youthful member for Elgin (Mr. Crothers). Apart from the placer yield of the country there are the most wonderful deposits of quartz. You cannot turn in any direction without finding quartz leads, quartz ledges, and stringers, which were it not for the excessive cost of transportation would be developed at once. We have scores and scores of mines which were they situated at an accessible place would to-day be developed and yielding profits. There are, however, mines at the threshold of the territory at Carcross which are being developed. No enormous amount has been expended upon them because in the development of a large mine half a million dollars is inconsiderable, but, they will no doubt greatly add to the mineral wealth of that territory. Then you pass to Whitehorse and you have at a crescent of territory twenty-five miles in extent on which you can scarcely go 200 yards without finding outcrop of copper of the highest grade. Recently on the dome between Hunker and Dominion Creeks they have struck at one place on the 550 foot level and at another place at the 100 foot level indications of the good paying quartz. Last summer from the Mackenzie river side, the prospectors returned with specimens of some of the richest quartz ever known. Of course I do not know whether it will turn out as anticipated, but at all events the existence of these minerals In every quarter shows that the mining industry in the Yukon territory is practically only in the same initial stage that it is in British Columbia and in Ontario. I do not think it would be rash to say that within twenty-five years Canada will exceed any country in the world in its mineral production. Then, experience has taught us, as in the case of the northern regions, and Cobalt, and Gowganda, that the best thing to promote settlement in a territory is mineral discovery, because the minerals will not only yield wealth themselves but they will bring in population which will remain there to develop agriculture and other natural resources. The subject is perhaps more entertaining to me than it is to the members of the House, and I must apologize for detaining hon. gentlemen at such length, but at all events I feel confident that the Yukon territory deserves the encouragement of the government and of the country in the development of its extraordinarily rich resources.

The budget debate, Mr Speaker, is a wonderful institution. It allo-ws the erudite scholar to exhibit his knowledge ^of the dead languages, and to some others it gives the opportunity to exnose their dense ignorance as to the conditions of this country. It appears to me that it is largely used by hon. gentlemen opposite to vie with one another in lavishing praise on the present administration; and I have no doubt that they have succeeded in impressing on our cabinet ministers the conviction that to their administration is due every advantage which the country now enjoys. To their wisdom is due everything from the copious rains that have blessed our soil as well as the withholding from the supposedly free citizens of Ottawa their rights and privileges in this House. Judging by this debate, we have to wander abroad in order to learn some things of our own country. I have lived in the west a considerable number of years and thought I knew something about it, but this debate has revealed some wonderful things about

it. We have heard a great deal about the railway development in that country, and I would like to give to the House some experience respecting the constituency I represent, a constituency consisting of 16,000,000 acres of land, or something over 25,000 square miles. When the Conservative party went out of power in 1896, there were 350 miles of railway in operation in that constituency. Since then there has been added, during all these years of peace and plenty, some 80 or 90 miles of railway to the mileage then in operation. We all know that the Railway Department receives statements from the railway corporations on the 30th of June each year, giving their mileage. I have not the figures before me, but I know that the statements made to the Railway Department on the 30th June, 1908 and 1909, in so far as Alberta is concerned, do not show the increase of one mile of railway, while in the province of Saskatchewan some 500 or 600 miles were added during 1909. We all know that railways are being built in Alberta as well as Saskatchewan; I merely mention these figures to show the preponderance of railway construction in Saskatchewan over that in Alberta.
Now, I had not the slightest thought of taking part in this debate, nor would I do so now were it not that the Minister of Finance, in his budget speech, made certain references to the postal revenues with which I cannot agree. And I feel that I would not he doing my duty to the people who sent me here if I allowed the views thus expressed to go unchallenged. There was evident pleasure in the announcement of that hon. gentleman that the policy of hi's government-a policy which undertakes to make money out of the Post Office -had yielded him such a handsome profit. Last session, when he was engaged in a similar task, I very well remember-if I may so put it-his gleeful reference to the splendid surplus from that department. The late administration has been criticised in this House and in the country because it conducted the Post Office Department with a deficit. I am not so sure that we should criticise that government for such a policy. I hold the opinion that an intelligent government, in upbuilding a young country, should not attempt to turn shekels from the post office into the treasury. We might as well turn our .militia service into a money-making establishment. I assume we are an intelligent people. I presume the Minister of the Interior is endeavouring to get intelligent people to come into this country with whom we will share our citizenship. And I believe that one of the requisites of an intelligent people is an up-to-date mail service, in other words, I believe that the intelligence of a country, to a large extent, is measured by the char-61

acter of its mail service. We invite people to come here and settle upon our undeveloped areas, and turn over the sod. They are the men who are making Canada. We ask them to take their families away from older settled sections in other countries, to deprive them of the privileges and comforts that they enjoy there and to go out pioneering for us, in short, to turn their backs upon civilization and to go forty or fifty or seventy miles away from railway facilities. And when they ask us to give them a new post office or more frequent service than a weekly one, I say we are not justified in sometimes returning the answer that the service will not warrant the expenditure-in other words, that the service must be self-supporting. In support of that statement, I wish to read an extract from a letter recently received from the Post Office Department:
The offers received for the performance of the mail service to the proposed office, are moreover so high as compared with the probable revenue of the office as to render it impossible for the department to consider the establishment of a post office at this point at present,
I do not think it necessary to refer to other communications, but merely read that one in justification of the statement I made. Besides, we are specifically taxing the periodicals which follow our settlers from the United States into our country. I have before me an account rendered against myself by the ' Literary Digest,' published in the city of New York, the annual subscription to which is $3. That figure wdi deliver it in England, in Alaska or anywhere in the United States. But the first item that I see on this account is ' Canadian postage, 85 cents '-or 28 per cent of. the price that will deliver it ten times further than Canada. And this has to be borne by the subscribers in this country on account of the regulations of our post office. If hon. gentlemen opposite wish to throw up their hats because of the results of the post office service, we have excellent opportunity to see how they are obtained, and for my part, I do not believe in such a system. The United States does not assume to tax the papers which follow our people who settle in their country-and I wish to announce that there are a few people going out of this country as well as coming in. The United States does not attempt to turn its post office service into a money-making establishment, and I do not think we should attempt it either. I am very sorry that the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) is not in his seat. I told him this afternoon that I wished to make reference to some matters in his department. I believe that the officials of his department are doing all in their power to serve the public; I have no complaint to make against the officials.

Nor have I any complaint to make against the Postmaster General, but wish to acknowledge the courtesy he extends to me from his seat in this House. But when it comes to another feature of his administration, the political end of it, I am determinedly opposed to the system. I believe that in a free country like this, our Post Office Department should be organized free of political managers. I believe that local pooh-bahs should not be appointed as dispensers of post offices. If the people elect a representative to this House and select wisely but not well according to hon. gentlemen opposite, then there is a gentleman in the west selected as a pooh-bah, as purveyor of post offices. I have evidence of this-any quantity of it. And I say that this is wrong. It is immaterial to me what government adopts that policy, I say that the sooner it is changed the better it will 'be for a young country like Canada. I would like to see the Postmaster General place .more post office inspectors at work in the west. And when a petition for a post office is handed in, if the inspector, on looking over the ground, states that a post office should be established and that John Smith would be a good man to appoint as postmaster, that should settle the matter clear of politicians. That is what the country wants. I received letters from the Postmaster General last session in which he informed me that he had done certain things and added .a paragraph to the effect that he had done so at the request of a gentleman in the constituency whom he evidently constituted a purveyor of post offices. I do not object, to any one assisting in securing a post office; it is a matter of indifference to me who helps to get it or by whom it is secured so long as it is secured. I wonder if the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) has the idea .that unless he puts such a paragraph in his letters, I will go into my constituency and say to the people: ' I have got the Widow Jones this post office at the munificent sum of $10 ia year? ' so that they will think I am a wonderful individual, or that
I will try to impress the man who is keeping a stopping place at which the mail service passes once a week that I am ia wonderful individual because I have succeeded in getting a service twice a week, whereby he is able to sell double the amount of oats for the mail driver's horses, which gives him that additional profit. If that is the conception of the Postmaster General as to the duties of a public man in this country, I may say that I do not see eye to eye with him.

There is another matter to which I would like to refer briefly. We are frequently told that Canada is a great country. Unquestionably she is possessed of great natural resources, of vast virgin wealth. But if she is going to be great, she is already on the highroad towards great and grave crises. We need not attempt to overlook that, because the fact is evident. Great internal questions will arise, and none more important perhaps than the conservation of our natural resources for the people, so that predatory wealth may not get loose among our natural resources, as it unfortunately has done to a considerable extent in the United States. Then we will have great issues to settle with our neighbours, and with other countries. Let me take the case of a great industry which employs to look after its interests a prominent legal firm, which knows the business of that corporation from the ground up. Now, if that firm should have some legal controversy with another firm, its solicitors will be able to look after its interests properly. Now to what extent are we moving in that direction? Very slowly, so far as I can see. It is a great pleasure to me to visit the campus of some of our universities and see the young men they are turning out. It is a refreshing sight to see the photographs of the faculties of our different universities. They are loaded with intelligence. The young men who pass out of those universities are absorbed, largely, into our commercial and professional life, while many of them leave the country. Now, Mr. Speaker, I would be delighted to see this government make some arrangement with the presidents of our universities for throwing a mesh around the graduating classes in say, arts and engineering, and what the sieve held back to throw some of them into our Archives, and keep them there for a few years under proper direction, investigating old treaties, &c. Sir, if wa should do that it would return usl our expenditure ten times, nay, a hundred times, more than such a service would cost us. Let us start in this country an engineering branch, an engineering board, as other countries have done. These men will be of great utility to the nation when important questions come up in this country for consideration. If we could breed such an investigating force into the life of this country, it would mean much for Canada-that is, if we are going to be a great people; of Mr. MAGRATH.
course, if we are not going to be a great people, it is unnecessary to look into the future. But I believe we should do it, and if we do, my opinion is there will in the future be less opportunity to make the charge that Great Britain ha3 surrendered our rights in an attempt to appease some other nation.
I want to offer a few remarks regarding our outside service. A few years ago, previous to the last general election, we had the inside service placed under a commission. The outside service is still in the same old condition. The members of the inside service were advised that they were to receive an increase in salary previous to election. The outside service have not been so treated. Unfortunately for them they are not hived together in any locality, but I believe, Sir, it is our duty to place the outside service under a commission and to do it at once. If they have any rights, if they are entitled to increases, by all means let them have increases, but put them in a position in which they can be properly looked after. I occasionally visit the public accounts committee of this House of parliament and I see some things that are not particularly agreeable to me as a citizen of this country. I see officials of the outside service brought before that committee. I have in my mind at the present time an instance in which a gentleman who almost forgot his name when under examination by hon gentlemen opposite on this side of the House but, when he happened to be taken in hand by hon. gentlemen opposite it took almost twenty gentlemen to carry away what he had to give. Was that gentleman so seriously to blame? It is true that he gave his sacred oath that he would tell the truth and nothing but the truth, but I fear very much, Sir, that he juggled with the truth. His bread and butter was at stake with the political head of his department gazing into his countenance conveying the intelligence that if he should allow himself to give away any idea that should injure the government his official position would not be worth the paper on which it was written. Was that right? I do not care what government is in power, the system is wrong. Probably that man has a family whose bread and butter is at stake. Let us get these things right because I realize that political parties are drawn from the people of this country and that the same policy might result in the same effects. I am not going to make an admission of that sort, but it is probable and we want on this side of the House to see that method done away with.
We had the sight in this House some few weeks ago of no less a personage than the Prime Minister so entangled in the rules and regulations that he could not get

footloose in order to let the people of the city of Ottawa have their proper representation in this House. 1 am not going to say anything against the premier. I have no thought or desire to do it, but I am going to say something else. Where do the people of Ottawa come in? The criticism is too frequently levelled at public men in this country that they are not doing their duty. I would like to know what the people of Ottawa have been doing all this time. Has there been any effort on their part to have this matter rectified? As far as I can see there has not. I may be treading on dangerous ground but the spice of life comes to a man who steps out of the beaten track and freely expresses his views and I want the people of Ottawa to know my view of the matter. If that condition of affairs existed in the city of London there would be a few processions passing back and forth in front of the Prime Minister's door in Downing street, and I think that if we had that kind of energy shown by the people in this new country it would be better for the country.
I do not see my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) in his seat, but I want to offer him my condolences, because I think I can sincerely offer them, in the loss of the deputy minister of Railways and Canals. The business of this government is the biggest business in the country and it is an astonishing state of affairs that the largest corporation-the country itself-can afford to allow smaller corporations to take from them men of that character. I suppose it is done by paying them more money. I say it is regrettable that this gentleman should be allowed to pass out of the service of this country.
I have had the pleasure of meeting him occasionally, and I feel that we had occupying this position a gentleman of the very highest ability and a credit to whoever selected him for the place. I have had a very high opinion of him and not only of him but of many others among the deputy ministers. I merely w'anted to put myself on record in that respect. Now, Sir, I have nothing further to say and I thank the hon. gentlemen for the attention they have given me.

Mr. Speaker, with the year 1908 the whole world entered into a most difficult period for industry and commerce.
Throughout the economic crisis, Canada has been able to preserve unscathed her financial prestige, and the people at large are- to be congratulated upon their steadfastness in the midst of numerous diffieul ties. Our financial institutions have, by their prudent, skilful and enlightened policy avoided economic disaster. They now require from the government the opening of new avenues for the extension of our trade,
in order to be able to compete successfully against the organized effort of foreign nations.	.	.	.
Foreign trade is a sure indication of the progress or decadence of any nation. There can therefore be no financial question of more paramount importance than the choice of our commercial representatives in the different countries with which we trade.
On May 14, 1909, we had seventeen trade commissioners and six commercial agents-abroad. Did those gentlemen possess the requisite qualifications for the promotion of our commerce? Are they in a position to enlighten us as to the best means of shaping the. national effort on the newest lines of production and sale? The greater nations have commercial representatives stationed systematically in all civilized countries. They are the great commercial travellers of trade and industry. Such servants of the state must be active and disinterested instruments of our commercial expansion. _
In every country with which we trade in agricultural or manufactured products, om-commercial agents should be men of good education and well informed as to our natural wealth and economic conditions. To Canada, the markets of Great Britain and of the United States are at present the most important. But we have only four commercial agents in the British Isles, and none in the United States, in Belgium or in Germany. We desire to extend our trade with France, but we have only one commercial agent at Paris. Every country desirous of extending its trade relations should secure influential commercial representatives.
A magnificent future may be reserved to the foreign trade of the Dominion if we make an effort towards training young men for such service, and take care to send out only carefully selected persons.
Our universities taking, as they do, so constant an interest in the progress of the Canadian people, might undertake the training of young men for our commercial and consular service.
If we desire that our agricultural, forest and mining products should be disposed of to the best advantage, we should endeavour to improve and perfect the means of transportation. During the financial year 1908-9, the ordinary and special expenditures of the country amounted to $126,000,000, and the public debt was increased by $45,000,000. ., Among the special expenditures, those incurred by the construction of the National Transcontinental were the most important; they amounted to $24,892,351 during the fiscal year. This year we will spend, under the same head, twentv millions, and during the fiscal year 1910-11, twenty-seven millions.

In his opening remarks, the hon. member urged the necessity of further extending our commercial relations with foreign countries and of organizing a thorough system of consuls and commercial agents. The thing exists already, and though it may not he as perfect as the same institutions in other great countries, we have good reasons to believe that before long Canada will have its own diplomatic service for administrative and commercial purposes, and that legislation to that end will be submitted to the sanction of the electors, through their representatives in parliament.
That question is not a new one; it has been discussed before. I remember that when it was proposed to have a Canadian attache at the English embassy in the United States, to watch Canadian interests in that country, the right hon. Prime Minister stated that the time had not come yet for a change. I do not think it would be proper for me to go beyond that statement made by the man entrusted with the administration of this country.
The hon. member for I,'Islet, speaking of the National Transcontinental, said it was a national, a necessary and an indispensable enterprise. That admission on his part may go a long way to atone for a lot of sms of a party that for years has assailed the policy of the government in this matter. To-day it is readily admitted that the construction of that road must be pushed to completion as rapidly as possible, and that, as a consequence. it is necessary to provide the means, that is to say, the large sums without which it is not possible to complete a work of such magnitude.
I am totally in accord with the hon. member for L'Islet when he states that the progress of the city of Quebec is essential to the progress, the expansion and the development of eastern Canada. It is indispensable that we should have a connecting link between the city of Quebec and eastern Canada, and the construction of the Quebec bridge is an absolute necessity for the commercial and industrial development of the country.
I admit, that a serious accident has occurred, and I have even heard an hon. member on the other side jeering at the matter. But an accident can be overcome, and the more so with a government such as the one which presides over the destinies of the country. The greatest, misfortune can then he overcome, and that is the reason whv, at this very session, we have in the estimates a vote of one million dollars for the preliminary disbursements entailed hv the reconstruction of the Quebec bridge. I have not the least doubt that the money will be

voted without discussion, as it is the first step in the improvement of our transportation system.
The honourable member for l'lslet has also criticised the management of the Intercolonial. I feel rather inclined to share his views; still, if there have been deficits, it is not owing to the Liberal government's policy, but to that of the preceding Conservative governments. Since many years, the tradition of deficits has been transmitted by the Conservative governments that consecutively managed this line. A known fact is, that much efforts are being done towards covering those deficits, and amending the management generally.
I do not pretend that the work of reform undertaken by the hon. Minister of Railways shall at once put an end to the deficits of the Intercolonial; but, what I believe, and what seems to be the prevailing opinion of the moment is, that the information of a special commission such as the one appointed, is bound to bring the railway on the basis of a financial business. I do not mean to say that this commission has given everybody satisfaction, not in the manner in which the line has been managed by its members-I do not pretend that perfection has crowned the first efforts-as perfection does not exist in the world-but I state that under the circumstances, the creation of a commission formed of four members to manage this line constitutes a remarkable progress compared to the old system; it shows how anxious this government is to put an end to a very bad management.
The complaints on the members of this commission were filed independently of the channel of the member for l'lslet, and that, long ago. It is possible that the government met with unavoidable obstacles in the pursuance of its policy. There is a favourable occasion to redress a mistake or do what has been, so far, forgotten, and we think, on this side of the House, that the government will rectify such mistake or do what had been forgotten. We trust the government to'be very just, and we believe that if wrongs exist, they shall be promptly redressed, since a favourable occasion is presently at hand. As regards the formation of this commission, we are all of opinion-not only the French-speaking members, but the English members also- that this board of management for national railways should contain at least one French commissioner. This request was often made in my presence, and I know it is the government's intention to grant it.
As a member of an agricultural county, it seems to me, that when the times comes to furnish the government with the necessary sums to administer the affairs of the country for the coming fiscal year, it is
not strictly urgent to study, to weigh all the theories concerning free trade and protection, or to go backward to see if the methods of the past were ahead of or worse than the present. The pe.ople, whose attributions are to decide about these matters every four or five years, determine to the best of their judgment what party is more fit to hold the power. Now, one party has the supremacy, then it is the other. In certain details the methods are somewhat different; practically, I believe that the fundamental principles of the administration are the same with either party in power. What is certain, since 1896, when the actual government took the reins, the people thought the public affairs well directed since the same men were elected three or four different times to attend to public interests. Nobody, I think, except those whose ambition is to see the power come to their side-nobody, I think, amongst the people, has complained that the management was bad or dishonest and contrary to the pubic interest.
In the objections filed by the members of the opposition, what is most remarkable is that they each have their sore spot, and think they have discovered something crooked in the management of this country or region. But, as regards the country generally as a nation, the depression which was talked about does not exist either in commerce or in the industries, and as far as the citizen's pride is concerned, nothing shows that the people is wrongly governed nor that he has reasons to complain of the administration. It is all the contrary, it seems that the commerce is taking much extension, that industry is more active and makes much progress and that the neople is generally satisfied of its lot. I do not pretend that this state of affairs is totallv and exclusively due to the government; I don't belong to the class of people who believe that the governments can make the people happy or unhappy, prosperous or not; but on the other hand, I believe that in a society such as ours, where aspirations are apt to cause frictions and sometimes much dissentions, much credit is due to those who hold the power to administer the business of this immense country without bringing conflict amongst these different aspirations, but on the contrary to help to the harmony which contributes to the general welfare. It is the state of affairs that we witness actually, and as far as the agricultural counties are concerned, those on which the government is supposed to bestow more attention, I feel satisfied that things are going altogether well.
I know very well that the supporters of the protection nolicv who sip on the other side of the House would like to see a higher tax put on foreign industrial products. Thev are of oninion that it would be an issue to develop our national indus-

try, and that, consequently the farmers would have the benefit of it. The interests of the greater number is to be taken into consideration would be the answer to that argument which seems to be somewhat catchy.
All the question would be to find out whether the producers are more numerous than the consumers. As the industrial class is limited, and the consumers account for nearly the entire population, a financial standing for this country should be such as to give satisfaction to the larger portion of the ponulation and to prevent any complaint from the consumers. It is an unquestioned fact that when protection was in full swing, at the time when scandalous fortunes were accumulated by the owners of industries, it is exactly the time when the mass of consumers were most unhappy, it was at that time also that the farm products were sold at the lowest figure, this statement is supported by the statistics.
I therefore, believe that the government, while imposing taxes sufficient to cover the expenses of administration without favouring the manufacturer at the expense of the consumer acted wisely. The great powers of Europe have been spoken of ; it has been stated that they were surrounded by protection, and in spite of that, strange to say, the money obtained that way by their government has been spent at the expense of the welfare of the public. For instance-and I am going to aeal now with the question of militarism, the plague of Europe-which will soon be put forward as a stepping stone to frighten the people of this country, is it not a fact that the largest part of those incomes levied in order to encourage industry, has been spent in huge armaments, for the maintenance of troops brought together by compulsory service laws leaving their country in a state of poverty, after spending foolishly to a certain extent the money paid in by the people.
